A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adaptive Robust Clipping (ARC) work despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v3 reports original image-classification experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, including attack, heterogeneity, clipping, and initialization comparisons.

after.justification: v5 retains original classification results and reports additional static-clipping comparisons, larger-system experiments, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same procedures. ARC still clips the largest floor(2(f/n)(n−f)) gradients at the next-largest norm. Appendix A.1 explains this choice without changing the implemented algorithm; the ResNet-18 configuration was already described in v3.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same three classification datasets, heterogeneity regimes, and five attack families. v3 Appendix F.1 already describes Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 static-clipping experiments. Newly displayed results and larger worker counts extend evidence and settings within this coverage.

E2.justification: v5 Figure 26 introduces a direct runtime comparison between ARC and standalone NNM, previously used as a pipeline component. The accuracy-comparison families remain CWTM, GM, CWMed, MK, static clipping, no clipping, and Byzantine-free DSGD. Relocating CWMed/MK results does not remove those comparators.

E3.justification: v5 adds MNIST experiments with 30 honest workers and f = 3, 6, 9; CIFAR-10 experiments with 33 honest workers; and additional adversarial-worker counts with 16 honest workers. Figure 26 introduces controlled runtime sweeps over model dimension and worker count. These substantially extend evaluation settings while retaining the existing training budgets and preprocessing.

E4.justification: v5 adds reported static-threshold sensitivity comparisons on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, tests robustness in larger systems, and measures computational scaling. Conversely, v3 Figure 18's honest-gradient norm histogram is removed. The initialization-sensitivity study and most earlier attack analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.4 in both versions specifies seeds 1–5 and standard deviations across those seeds. The added accuracy tables follow the existing reporting practice; no increased run count, significance testing, or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v5 adds substantial results in Tables 3–4 and 6–7 and the larger-system and runtime figures. Original Table 1 values remain unchanged across v5 Tables 1 and 5. Added results are not uniformly favorable: Table 6 reports GM accuracy of 49.6 ± 1.4 with ARC versus 50.9 ± 2.5 without clipping for f = 3 and alpha = 0.5. These are new results, not deterioration under a matched v3 setting.

T1.justification: Appendix C corrects the norm-ordering inequalities in the proof of Lemma 5.1 from ascending to descending. Section 5.1 adds a derivation of the admissible adversarial-worker interval and its integer-count implications. The principal theorem statements, assumptions, and proof strategies remain unchanged.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that ARC preserves robustness guarantees, improves convergence under suitable initialization, and strengthens empirical robustness particularly under heterogeneity and adversarial pressure. The revised title and abstract preserve these contributions; added experiments support existing claims.

C2.justification: v5 newly explains that Theorem 5.2's improvement interval can contain at most one integer adversarial-worker count in small systems, and removes the blanket statement that ARC has no downside. Appendix A.1 adds design rationale, while Section 6 identifies privacy-preserving use as requiring further analysis.

D1.justification: v5 Tables 3–4 newly specify CIFAR-10 static thresholds of 0.05, 0.5, 5, and 50; the associated ResNet-18 training details already appeared in v3. v5 also removes Appendix D.4's direction to supplementary per-dataset plot folders. Neither change establishes that resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds positioning relative to privacy and Byzantine robustness, citing works including Abadi et al., Guerraoui et al., Zhu and Ling, and Choffrut et al. The introduction also adds El-Mhamdi et al. The central distinctions from prior adaptive-clipping methods remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract and substantial empirical prose are rewritten, and Section 4 is reorganized into static-clipping and no-clipping comparisons. Appendices E and F exchange roles and are reorganized by dataset and system size. Together these materially restructure the presentation despite stable core scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 Figure 17 becomes main-text Figure 2, Figure 1 moves to Appendix E, and Figure 5 is incorporated into v5 Figure 23. Table 1 is split between the main text and appendix, several panel arrangements change, and new tables and plots are added. The gradient-norm histogram is removed; retained plot content otherwise matches.

improvement.justification: v5 strengthens empirical support through previously unreported static-clipping results, larger-system tests, and runtime measurements. The practical-scope discussion and proof correction improve precision. These are incremental gains over an already developed paper: the method and principal results remain stable, one explanatory histogram is lost, and exceptions in Table 6 limit the retained language of consistent superiority.
